newsitem.title: UK: Lloyd's chief calls for strategy rethink.
newsitem.headline: Lloyd's chief calls for strategy rethink.

text.p: Lloyd's of London chief executive Ron Sandler called on Tuesday for a radical overhaul of the insurance market's decision making processes.
He told delegates at a conference in London that a greater sense of unity among members was needed for effective leadership.

Sandler gave the strongest indication yet that a wide-ranging review of how Lloyd's operated might extend beyond the regulatory system and efficiency of services the market provides to embrace its complex management structure.

With the recovery plan complete and terrible losses of previous years consigned to history, Lloyd's is turning its attention to the future. Many of the challenges it faces are still, however, of a very significant and pressing nature.
The insurance market now wants to look again at the way its ruling council, market board and committees are structured.

Sandler said this in part stemmed from a need to reflect changes in Lloyd's capital structure. The market has witnessed an influx of corporate investment over recent years, replacing the traditional individual backers called Names.
Around 40 percent of the capital underpinning Lloyd's next year is expected to come from corporate investors with limited liability, who this year account for 30 percent of capacity.
The numbers of Names have meanwhile been declining. Down from over 30,000 in the late 1980s, about 2,000 of the 12,500 still active may leave Lloyd's at the end of this year.
Sandler expressed concern that the sense of community which has bound the society together may have weakened, undermining one of the market's traditional fundamental strengths.
"The willingness to make the sacrifice for the greater good appears to be less present and the introduction of corporate capital has introduced considerable new tensions into the society," he said.
"I am concerned about whether we have sufficient in the way of shared value and common purpose to allow a cohesive vision to be created and for effective leadership to operate."

"For this reason, I believe that a rethink of the governance of the society to take into account the new world that we have entered is an essential step in the on-going process of renewal. And furthermore, we need to take it soon."

The present executive apparatus at Lloyd's was designed to separate the business of market issues from regulation. A review of the regulatory system is under way, and appointments to a new regulatory review panel are expected shortly. This may see some responsibility for investor protection moving outside Lloyd's.
Sandler said he expected to see far fewer than 45 new syndicates formed next year -- the upper end of an estimated range circulating in Lloyd's underwriting circles recently.

He said he expected to see around half that number. Some of these were likely to be the new underwriting entities resulting from syndicate mergers announced earlier this year, in addition to so-called "parallel" syndicates for some corporate investors.
